Edmund Husserl

Edmund Husserl (1859–1938) founded phenomenology as a rigorous method for investigating the structures of conscious experience 1, 2. Every conscious act has a noetic aspect (the act of perceiving, judging, remembering) and a noematic aspect (the content perceived, judged, remembered). His analyses of internal time-consciousness—how the mind holds together the just-past (retention), the living present (primal impression), and the about-to-come (protention)—describe the temporal microstructure of experience in terms deeply compatible with predictive processing’s account of temporal prediction.

John Dewey

John Dewey (1859–1952), in his landmark critique of the reflex arc concept 3, argued that perception and action are not separate stages in a linear chain but phases of a continuous organism–environment loop. The stimulus does not precede the response; the organism’s ongoing activity determines what counts as a stimulus. This circular causality between perception and action is a core motif of modern active inference and enactivism.

Martin Heidegger

Martin Heidegger (1889–1976) rejected the entire framework of a subject representing an external world. In Being and Time 4, human existence (Dasein) is always already being-in-the-world—embedded, practical, and engaged. We encounter objects primarily as ready-to-hand (zuhanden)—tools transparently integrated into purposive action—rather than as present-at-hand (vorhanden)—detached objects of theoretical scrutiny. The latter arises only in breakdown. For world-modeling theories, Heidegger poses a challenge: if our primary mode of engagement is skilled, transparent coping, is an internal model always involved, or only when things go wrong?

Ludwig Wittgenstein

Ludwig Wittgenstein (1889–1951) offered two profoundly different philosophies of mind. The Tractatus 5 proposed a picture theory of meaning: propositions are logical pictures of states of affairs, their structure mirroring the structure of the world. The later Philosophical Investigations 6 dismantled this image: meaning is constituted by use within social language games, not by correspondence between inner representations and outer facts. His discussion of seeing-as (the duck–rabbit figure), and the private language argument—which challenges the coherence of a purely internal, first-person mental vocabulary—raises deep difficulties for any theory that grounds world modeling in private neural representations alone.

Rudolf Carnap

Rudolf Carnap (1891–1970), in Der logische Aufbau der Welt 7, attempted to rationally reconstruct all concepts of science from a base of elementary experiences (Elementarerlebnisse) using purely logical relations. The project is, in effect, a formal blueprint for building a hierarchical world model from sensory primitives—and its partial failure is instructive: Carnap discovered that logical construction from experience alone is insufficient without structural priors, an insight consonant with the Kantian foundations of predictive processing.

Bertrand Russell

Bertrand Russell (1872–1970) developed a form of neutral monism that dissolved the mind–body divide 8, 9. Both mental and physical events, he argued, are composed of the same underlying neutral “stuff”; the distinction between mind and matter is one of arrangement, not of intrinsic nature. A given event is “mental” when placed in the context of a particular biography (a chain of experiences) and “physical” when placed in the context of a causal group radiating from a spatial location. Russell also drew the influential distinction between knowledge by acquaintance (direct, non-inferential awareness of sense-data) and knowledge by description (indirect knowledge mediated by concepts and inference)—a divide that maps suggestively onto the difference between the brain’s raw sensory prediction errors and the high-level, structured world model that interprets them.

Wolfgang Köhler (1887–1967), together with Max Wertheimer and Kurt Koffka, founded Gestalt psychology on the principle that perceptual experience is organized into structured wholes (Gestalten) that are irreducible to the sum of their sensory elements 10, 11. The laws of perceptual grouping—proximity, similarity, closure, good continuation, common fate, Prägnanz—describe the structural priors the visual system brings to the organization of sensory input, segmenting the retinal image into objects, surfaces, and events before any deliberate analysis. Köhler’s principle of psychophysical isomorphism proposed that the structural relations within perceptual experience faithfully mirror the structural relations within the underlying brain dynamics—a hypothesis that finds modern expression in topographic cortical maps, representational similarity analysis, and the geometry of neural population codes.
